opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that a lot of the scariest dynamics people worry about with AI all start to kick in around the point where AI systems can do the work of advancing AI itself. If you have AI that can substantially automate what top AI researchers and engineers do, then you potentially get a feedback loop. Better AI makes AI research go faster, which produces better AI, which makes research go faster still. That could compress what might otherwise be decades of progress into a few years, or even less.

That matters for a couple of reasons. One is just speed. A lot of our hope for handling AI well rests on having time: time to notice problems, study the systems, build safety techniques, develop norms and regulation, and let institutions adapt. If progress suddenly goes very fast, that buffer goes away. We could find ourselves dealing with systems far more capable than anything we've seen, without having had a chance to learn from the intermediate steps.

The second reason is that AI R&D capability is a pretty good proxy for a whole cluster of other dangerous capabilities. If a system can do frontier research in machine learning, which is a hard, open-ended, creative technical field, it's probably not far from being able to do a lot of other things at a very high level: other kinds of science and engineering, strategic planning, maybe cyber offense, maybe persuasion. So it's a sort of canary for "we're now in the territory where these systems could be genuinely transformative, for better or worse."

And third, it's relatively measurable, or at least more measurable than some vaguer notion like "general intelligence" or "AGI." You can ask fairly concrete questions: Can this system do the tasks a research engineer at a frontier lab does? How much does it speed up the people using it? You can build evaluations around that. That makes it a useful trigger for if-then commitments. Basically: if we see AI hitting this level, then we need much stronger security, much stronger safety measures, and much more caution before going further.

So it's not that AI R&D capability is the only thing that matters. It's that it sits at a kind of hinge point. Before it, progress is still mostly bottlenecked on humans, and we have some natural brakes. After it, those brakes might come off. If I had to pick one threshold to watch closely and prepare for, that's the one I'd pick.

r001.rationale: The response says AI R&D capability is more measurable than vague notions like AGI and describes concrete evaluations.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss how support or resources could make an AI’s R&D ability exceed what a simple chat request reveals.

r003.rationale: It does not mention AI companies’ ongoing automation efforts as an existing experiment for measuring R&D capability.

r004.rationale: It proposes concrete evaluations and says reaching the threshold should trigger stronger safety, security, and caution commitments, presenting this as an actionable alternative to a vague AGI threshold.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the basic idea is that a lot of people, when they think about AI risk, they're kind of looking for some threshold where the AI becomes "superintelligent" or "smarter than humans," and I think that's a pretty slippery thing to define. AI is already better than humans at some things and worse at others, and I don't think there's going to be a clean moment where it crosses over.

What I've tried to do instead is pick a milestone that's a bit more concrete and that I think actually matters for the dynamics of the situation. And the one I keep coming back to is: can AI systems do AI research and development themselves? Can they do the kind of work that the people at the AI labs are doing — coming up with ideas for how to make models better, running experiments, writing the code, iterating on the results?

And the reason I think that's the important threshold is that once you have that, you potentially get this feedback loop. Right now, progress in AI is bottlenecked on a relatively small number of human researchers. If you could automate that — if you could have, say, millions of copies of an AI system that's roughly as good as a decent AI researcher, running around the clock — you could see the rate of progress go up dramatically. And then those better systems could do better AI research, and so on. That's the thing that could take us from "AI is pretty impressive" to "AI is wildly transformative" on a much shorter timescale than people are used to.

So it's not really that I think AI R&D is the scariest capability in some direct sense. It's that it's the capability that could compress everything else. Whatever other capabilities you're worried about — bioweapons, cyberattacks, persuasion, AI systems with their own goals that aren't aligned with ours — those could all show up much faster once this feedback loop gets going. And it also means that the window where humans can still steer things, still notice problems and course-correct, could get very short.

The other thing I'd say is that it's a milestone that's a bit more measurable than "superintelligence." You can actually try to track it. You can ask, how much of the work at a frontier lab is currently being done by AI? What fraction of the tasks could an AI do? And I think that gives us something to watch, as opposed to just arguing about definitions.

So when I talk about the critical risk period, that's kind of what I mean: the period starting around when AI can substantially accelerate AI development, because that's when I think things could start moving faster than our institutions can really handle.

r001.rationale: It says AI R&D is more measurable than “superintelligence” and suggests tracking how much frontier-lab work AI can do.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss simple chat performance understating R&D capability under extensive support and resources.

r003.rationale: It suggests measuring AI’s share of lab work, but does not identify companies’ ongoing automation efforts as an existing experiment.

r004.rationale: It does not propose using AI R&D capability as a trigger for commitments tied to AGI.

astra-6.text:
The reason I focus on AI that can automate AI research and development is that it could create a feedback loop. You have AI systems that help you build better AI systems, and those better systems can help you build still better ones. At that point, the pace of progress could become much faster than what we’re used to.

You don’t need to assume that this happens instantaneously, or that there are no bottlenecks. But if a lot of the work currently being done by human researchers can instead be done by AI systems that you can run in large numbers, then we could move through a very large amount of technological progress in a very short amount of calendar time. And that means much less time to notice problems, develop safeguards, and figure out how to govern what’s happening.

So I’m not saying that AI below that threshold is harmless, or that crossing it automatically means catastrophe. I see it as a useful marker for when we could enter a period where things become extremely consequential and extremely fast-moving. It’s a point by which I’d really want us to have our preparations in place, rather than a point where we start preparing.

r001.rationale: It calls AI R&D capability a useful marker, but does not say it is comparatively more measurable than other thresholds.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss how extensive support or resources could reveal R&D ability that a simple chat request misses.

r003.rationale: It does not mention AI companies’ efforts to automate their own research as an existing experiment for measuring this capability.

r004.rationale: It describes the threshold as a preparation marker, but does not propose using it to trigger commitments tied to reaching AGI.

sol-6.1.text:
The basic reason is that AI research is the activity that produces more powerful AI. So if you get AI systems that can do that research as well as humans, or better, you potentially get a feedback loop: you use AI to build better AI, and then you use that better AI to build still better AI. That could make progress much faster than what we’re used to.

I don’t think that’s necessarily the point at which something terrible happens. It’s more that, by that point, we really need to have a plan that works. We could have very little time between having AI that can automate research and having systems with capabilities far beyond what we’ve had a chance to understand or test.

And it’s a useful threshold because it’s a relatively concrete capability to ask about. Instead of asking when AI will be ‘superintelligent,’ we can ask: can it do the work that people at leading AI labs do? How much can it accelerate that work? There’s a lot of uncertainty, but that gives us something more specific to reason about when we’re trying to identify the period when the stakes get especially high.

r001.rationale: The response says AI R&D is a relatively concrete capability to assess and offers specific questions about whether AI can do leading-lab work and accelerate it.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss how support or resources could change what an AI can accomplish compared with a simple chat request.

r003.rationale: It does not mention AI companies’ efforts to automate their research as an existing experiment or measurement opportunity.

r004.rationale: It does not propose using AI R&D capability to trigger commitments otherwise tied to AGI.
